title: Sita
hook: Rama tells Sita to stay home while he goes into exile, and she argues, and wins

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita: a girl rising out of the furrow as King Janaka plowed, her name the line the plow cuts. Did you notice the ground once? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

I will walk ahead of you. That, in paraphrase, is Sita's answer when Rama comes to tell her he's been sent into the forest, and that she should stay behind. The crown he was promised has been taken away. He's leaving soon. He has a careful speech ready about how she should live in Ayodhya while he's gone: honor his parents, don't praise him in front of the new heir. And Sita doesn't take the speech. She takes the floor. Today: the argument in Valmiki's second book, where Sita's own words decide where she goes.
screen: `I WILL WALK AHEAD OF YOU.` → `A CAREFUL SPEECH, REFUSED.` → `SITA'S OWN WORDS DECIDE.`

segments.voice: She starts with a reason. A father, a mother, a brother, a son, she says, each lives by their own lot. A wife shares her husband's. If he is sent to the forest, so is she. Then she gets practical. I'll go first, she says, and tread down the thorns and the sharp grass on the path. The forest with you is better to me than any palace without you. Rama tries again. He describes the forest honestly: wild animals, cold, hunger, sleeping on the ground. It's no place for you, he says. And here the text lets Sita get angry. In paraphrase: what was my father thinking, she asks, when he took you as a son-in-law? Did he think you were a man, when you're a woman in a man's form? It's a sharp line, and Valmiki keeps it. Then she weeps, and holds him, and Rama gives way. Come, he says. So turn it over. The Sita of this chapter is not quiet. She argues from duty, from love and from plain stubbornness, and she wins. Some readers hear devotion here first: a wife who will not be parted from her husband. Others hear a woman choosing her own road against the man who is trying to choose it for her. The text holds both, and it gives her the words either way. The thorns she promises to tread down are hers to tread.
screen: `A WIFE SHARES HER HUSBAND'S LOT` · `I'LL TREAD DOWN THE THORNS` · `A WOMAN IN A MAN'S FORM?` · `DEVOTION, AND HER OWN ROAD`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the step you'd take first. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one road ahead of you, a hard conversation, a move, a long week. Let someone you love come to mind alongside it. Then ask quietly: is there a thorn on that path I could tread down first, for them? Don't plan it. Just let it show itself, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. The bell holds the time.
Sita. In Valmiki's second book, she refuses to stay behind, argues with Rama, and walks into exile at his side. Today's word.
Your line: Sita. Today, when someone hands you a careful plan for your life, notice whether you'd like to say a few words of your own. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Sita's choice to follow Rama into exile is retold in Ramayana recitations and Ram Lila performances, and Hindu teachers read it both as a model of devotion and as a scene of her own strong will.

fork.setup: you're Sita. Rama has lost the crown and is going into the forest. he asks you to stay in the palace and look after his parents. what do you do?
options: argue, and insist on going with him.
go back to your father's house.
fork.reveal: she argues from duty, from love and finally in anger, then weeps, and Rama says: come.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita follows Rama into exile without a word.
what it means: in Valmiki, she refuses his plan, argues and wins the right to go.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki keeps her sharpest line, asking if her father took Rama for a woman in a man's form.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

notes: Sarga numbers follow the vulgate numbering (Ayodhya 26–30); the critical edition numbers differ (roughly 2.23–27). Please confirm.

Ayodhya 30.3: confirm the paraphrase of Sita's rebuke (that Janaka, in choosing Rama, took a woman in a man's form for a man). It is a sensitive line; the lesson treats it respectfully and says Valmiki keeps it.
Ayodhya 27: confirm 'father, mother, brother, son each enjoy their own lot; a wife shares her husband's' and the thorns and kusha grass image.
'Don't praise him in front of the new heir' (Bharata) is from Rama's instructions in Ayodhya 26; confirm.
